paragraphs.text: Most people who catch measles as children never catch it again, even if they are exposed to the virus many times later in life. This observation was made long before anyone understood why, and it lay behind some of the earliest attempts to prevent disease, including the ancient practice of deliberately exposing healthy people to material from mild cases of smallpox. Today the explanation is known in considerable detail. The immune system does not simply fight an infection and then return to its earlier state; it keeps a record of what it has encountered, and that record allows it to respond far more quickly and strongly the second time. Doctors in several ancient societies observed that people who survived certain diseases could safely nurse others with the same illness, and the same principle underlies every vaccine in use today.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first response to a new infection is slow. The general defences of the body, which attack anything that appears foreign, act within hours, but they are not specific and cannot always clear an infection alone. Fever and inflammation, which often accompany infection, are part of this general response. The specific response, carried out by white blood cells called lymphocytes, takes a week or more to build up. Among the millions of lymphocytes in the body, only a tiny number happen to carry receptors that fit a particular invader, and these few cells must be found, activated and multiplied into a large enough army to be effective.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Two kinds of lymphocyte do most of the work. B cells produce antibodies, proteins that attach to a virus or bacterium and either neutralise it directly or mark it for destruction by other cells. T cells have several roles: some coordinate the response, while others find and kill body cells that have already been infected. Once the infection has been cleared, most of the cells that multiplied to fight it die off, since maintaining such a large force would waste resources. B cells mature in the bone marrow, while T cells complete their development in a small organ in the chest called the thymus.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A minority, however, survive as memory cells. These long-lived cells, which remain in the blood, the bone marrow and the lymph nodes for years or even decades, retain the ability to recognise the same invader. If it returns, they multiply rapidly, and the antibodies they produce are often more effective than those made during the first infection, because the cells have undergone a process of refinement in which the best-fitting antibodies are selected. The second response can therefore eliminate an infection before it causes noticeable illness. Some memory cells stay in the tissues where the infection first occurred, ready to act at the point of entry.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Vaccines work by taking advantage of this memory. They expose the immune system to a harmless version or part of a disease-causing organism, such as a killed virus, a single protein from its surface or genetic instructions that lead the body to make that protein briefly. The immune system responds as it would to an infection, building a store of memory cells without the person having to suffer the disease. Some vaccines produce protection that lasts for life after one or two doses; others require regular boosters. Mass vaccination has eliminated smallpox entirely and made several other diseases rare in many countries, and vaccines are among the most thoroughly tested of all medical products.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Why memory lasts longer for some diseases than others is not fully understood. Immunity to measles, once established, appears to last for decades, whereas protection against some other infections fades within a few years. Part of the explanation lies in the organisms themselves. Influenza viruses change their surface proteins continually, so that memory cells produced against the strain of one year may not recognise the next, which is why the vaccine is updated regularly. Other viruses mutate slowly, allowing a single response to remain effective. Coronaviruses that cause common colds provide another example of immunity that seems to fade relatively quickly.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Memory can also be lost. Measles, ironically, is known to damage existing immune memory, wiping out part of the record of other infections a person has previously overcome, which may help to explain why children who have had measles are more vulnerable to other diseases for some time afterwards. Ageing reduces the production of new lymphocytes and the effectiveness of the response to unfamiliar infections, one reason why vaccines are sometimes less effective in older people and are given in stronger formulations. Some medicines that suppress the immune system, used after organ transplants, can also weaken memory.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Researchers continue to investigate how memory could be made more durable and broader. One goal is a vaccine that would protect against all strains of influenza by targeting parts of the virus that change little over time. Another is to understand why some people make much stronger memory responses than others, a question that involves both genetics and past exposure to infections. The basic principle, first exploited centuries before it was understood, remains among the most powerful tools in medicine. Researchers are also studying whether vaccines given through the nose could produce stronger memory in the airways.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Beneath most large cities lies a dense network of tunnels carrying trains, roads, water, sewage, electricity and data. Building them has always been among the most dangerous and difficult forms of engineering. Early tunnels were dug by hand, with workers breaking rock with picks or explosives and removing the debris in carts, and collapses and flooding were frequent. Workers also faced danger from bad air and from the high pressure used to keep water out. Today most urban tunnels are excavated by tunnel boring machines, enormous mechanical systems that cut, remove soil and build the tunnel lining in a single continuous process. Many of these tunnels are more than a century old and still in daily use.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The key invention came in the early nineteenth century, when an engineer building a tunnel under a major river in London devised a protective frame, known as a shield, within which workers could dig safely while the tunnel walls were built immediately behind them. According to a well-known story, he took the idea from a small marine creature that bores through wooden ships, protecting its head with a hard shell as it tunnels. The project took eighteen years and suffered several floods, but it proved that tunnelling through soft, wet ground was possible. The son of the engineer, who later became famous in his own right, worked on the project and was nearly killed in one of the floods.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Modern tunnel boring machines follow the same principle on a vastly larger scale. At the front, a rotating cutting head fitted with steel discs or teeth grinds into the ground. Behind it, the excavated material is carried back through the machine on conveyors or pumped away as a slurry. Immediately behind the cutting head, the machine installs curved concrete segments that lock together to form rings, creating the permanent lining of the tunnel. Hydraulic rams push against the completed rings to drive the machine forward, so that each finished section of tunnel provides the support for the next advance. The whole machine may be operated from a control cabin inside it, where screens show every part of the process, and crews work in shifts around the clock.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The ground itself determines much of the design. In hard rock, the cutting head grinds the face and the tunnel may need little additional support. In soft, water-bearing soil, the greatest danger is that the face will collapse or that water will pour in. Machines for such conditions keep the space in front of the cutting head under pressure, using either the excavated soil itself or a mixture of clay and water, so that the ground is held in place as it is dug. Sensors constantly monitor this pressure, since too little can cause collapse and too much can push up the ground above. Choosing the wrong type of machine for the ground can delay a project by months.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Tunnelling beneath a city carries a particular risk: the settlement of buildings above. Even small movements of the ground can crack walls or damage old structures with shallow foundations. Engineers survey buildings along the route before work begins, install instruments that measure movement to fractions of a millimetre, and in some cases inject grout beneath foundations to compensate for any sinking as the machine passes. The data are monitored around the clock, and the machine can be slowed or its settings changed if movements exceed agreed limits. Historic buildings are often given extra protection, including temporary supports inside them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The largest machines are among the biggest moving objects ever built. Some have cutting heads more than fifteen metres across, weigh several thousand tonnes and are longer than a football pitch when their support equipment is included. They typically advance between ten and thirty metres a day, although progress varies widely with ground conditions. Because they cannot easily be turned around, most are designed for a single project, and many are left buried or dismantled at the end of their tunnels. Some machines have been reused on later projects after being refurbished.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Machines are traditionally given names, often female names chosen by local people or schoolchildren, and many projects hold a ceremony before a machine begins work. The custom is said to derive from the tradition among miners of seeking the protection of a patron saint before going underground. Whatever its origin, it has become a way of involving the public in projects that otherwise take place entirely out of sight. Some machines have become minor celebrities, with their progress followed by local newspapers.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Despite these advances, tunnelling remains expensive and uncertain. Unexpected ground conditions, such as buried boulders, old foundations or pockets of water, can halt a machine for weeks, and cost overruns on major tunnel projects are common. Engineers are therefore investing in better ways of surveying the ground ahead of the machine, using techniques such as sound waves and drilling, so that the invisible obstacles that have troubled tunnellers for two centuries can be detected before they are reached. Digital models of the ground, updated as the machine advances, are also helping engineers to adjust their plans.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Is hydrogen the fuel of the future?

paragraphs.text: Hydrogen has been described as the fuel of the future for more than a century. It is the most abundant element in the universe, it can be burned or used in a fuel cell to produce electricity, and the only product of its use is water. In recent years governments have announced large programmes to develop a hydrogen economy, and companies have promised hydrogen-powered cars, trucks, ships, aircraft and home heating. Yet the enthusiasm has repeatedly outrun the results, and a growing number of analysts argue that hydrogen will play an important but much narrower role than its promoters suggest. Some estimates suggest that hydrogen could eventually supply around a tenth of the energy used in the world, and its supporters and critics now agree on more than they once did.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first difficulty is that hydrogen is not an energy source but a way of carrying energy. On Earth it is almost always bound to other elements, most commonly in water or natural gas, and energy must be spent to release it. Nearly all hydrogen produced today comes from natural gas in a process that releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. Hydrogen made by splitting water with renewable electricity, often called green hydrogen, produces no emissions, but it currently costs several times as much, and each conversion loses a substantial share of the original energy. Some hydrogen is also produced from natural gas with the carbon dioxide captured and stored, an approach whose climate benefit depends on how much gas leaks along the way.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Mei Lin, a chemical engineer, emphasises these losses. Turning electricity into hydrogen, storing and transporting it, and turning it back into electricity in a fuel cell typically wastes around two-thirds of the energy that went in. Using the same electricity to charge a battery wastes far less. In her view, hydrogen makes sense only where electricity cannot be used directly, since otherwise it squanders renewable power that could have displaced fossil fuels elsewhere. She also points out that renewable electricity is still scarce in many countries, so any that is wasted has a real cost. Supporters reply that surplus renewable power at times of low demand could be stored as hydrogen rather than wasted.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Storage and transport add further complications. Hydrogen is the lightest element and must be compressed to very high pressures or cooled to extremely low temperatures to be stored in useful quantities. It can leak through tiny gaps and make some metals brittle, which means that existing gas pipelines cannot always be reused without modification. Stefan Richter, an energy analyst, notes that these practical problems have made hydrogen refuelling stations expensive to build and operate, and that several countries have closed stations after demand failed to appear. Liquid hydrogen must be kept at temperatures colder than two hundred and fifty degrees below zero, and hydrogen flames are almost invisible in daylight, which adds to the safety challenge.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Transport illustrates the shift in expectations. Hydrogen cars were once expected to compete with battery-electric cars, but batteries have improved so quickly that most manufacturers have abandoned hydrogen passenger vehicles. Ama Owusu, who studies transport, argues that the case remains stronger for some heavy vehicles, such as long-distance trucks, but that even there batteries are advancing rapidly, and the outcome is uncertain. For shipping and aviation, fuels made from hydrogen, such as ammonia and synthetic kerosene, are considered more promising than hydrogen itself. Buses running on hydrogen have been tested in several cities, with mixed results.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The strongest case for hydrogen lies in industry. Hydrogen is already used in large quantities to make fertiliser and to refine oil, and replacing the fossil hydrogen currently used with green hydrogen would cut emissions without requiring new technology. Liam Walsh, an industrial economist, points out that hydrogen could also replace coal in steel-making, one of the largest sources of industrial emissions, and that several pilot plants are already producing steel in this way. He argues that public support should be concentrated on these uses, where there is no practical alternative. Fertiliser production alone uses more hydrogen than any other industry, and countries with abundant sunshine and wind hope to export green hydrogen or products made with it.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Home heating is the most disputed application. Some gas companies have proposed converting domestic gas networks to hydrogen, allowing existing boilers to be replaced rather than whole heating systems. Critics, including Lin, argue that heat pumps would provide the same heat using far less electricity, and trials in which villages were offered hydrogen heating have met local opposition. Richter adds that the safety of hydrogen in homes, where leaks could be difficult to detect, has not yet been demonstrated at scale. Some trials have been extended; others were cancelled.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Hydrogen is therefore unlikely to become the universal fuel that its most enthusiastic supporters once imagined. It is more likely to be used where it is hard to replace: in chemical industries, in steel-making and perhaps in some forms of heavy transport. Deciding where those limits lie, and concentrating investment accordingly, may prove more useful than continuing to promise that hydrogen will power everything. Its future, in other words, is real but specialised.
paragraphs.label: H
